meta.descriptionEn: On 31 October 2014, a rocket-powered spaceplane named VSS Enterprise was dropped from its mothership high above California's Mojave Desert. Seconds after its engine lit, something moved that should not have moved yet. Within moments the ship tore apart in the sky. This documentary follows the story from Richard Branson's bold promises and the early test flights, through a deadly 2007 explosion, years of engine troubles and delays, to the final seconds of the flight. We examine what the NTSB found about a premature feathering mechanism, a missing fail-safe, pilot training, and federal oversight. Could one human mistake really bring down a spaceship, or was something deeper wrong? Watch to find out what changed afterwards.
meta.descriptionUr: 31 October 2014 ko Mojave registan ke upar VSS Enterprise naam ka rocket se chalne wala spaceplane apne mothership se alag hua. Engine jalne ke chand lamhon baad woh hawa mein hi toot gaya. Is documentary mein hum Richard Branson ke bade wade, shuru ke test flights, 2007 ka dhamaka, engine ke masail aur aakhri lamhon ki kahani sunate hain. NTSB ne kya paya? Kya sirf ek insani ghalti zimmedar thi, ya design mein koi bari kami thi? Poori kahani dekhne ke liye video akhir tak zaroor dekhein.

articleEn: On the morning of 31 October 2014, preparations were complete for an important powered test flight over California's Mojave Desert. Mojave Air and Space Port sits in the desert. It is home to Scaled Composites, and it was where Enterprise's glide flights had landed.

That day, VSS Enterprise was flown slung beneath its mothership, WhiteKnightTwo. Enterprise was the first SpaceShipTwo. It was released at roughly 50,000 feet, and the pilots then ignited the rocket engine. Everything seemed to be going well. Then, roughly 60 to 90 seconds into the flight, an anomaly was reported, and the spaceplane was destroyed.

Pilot in command Peter Siebold managed to get out of the aircraft and later descended by parachute. Co-pilot Michael Alsbury, however, lost his life in the accident. He was 39 years old, and it was a huge loss. It was also the first spacecraft accident in which part of the crew survived, but not all of it, which gives the event a distinct place in history.

So the questions are these: what exactly moved too early? Was there no safeguard to prevent it? And what does all this mean for the dream of space tourism? Friends, this is not the story of a single accident. It is the story of many decisions.

articleEn: The story begins with the Ansari X Prize, a $10 million competition. The condition was that a non-government organization had to send a reusable crewed spacecraft into space twice within two weeks. The prize was created in May 1996, and on 6 May 2004 it was renamed after a donation from Anousheh Ansari and Amir Ansari. On 4 October 2004, the Tier One project won it. It was designed by Burt Rutan and financed by Paul Allen. The winning craft was SpaceShipOne, and its flights took place on 29 September and 4 October 2004. SpaceShipOne thus became known as the world's first private spaceship.

In that same year, 2004, Richard Branson founded Virgin Galactic. His company wanted to fly space tourists on suborbital flights. In 2005, The Spaceship Company was formed, with the Virgin Group holding 70 percent and Burt Rutan's Scaled Composites holding 30 percent. Virgin Galactic was the launch customer, and it agreed to buy five SpaceShipTwos and two WhiteKnightTwos. Scaled Composites was responsible for building the early prototypes. From 2008, The Spaceship Company began producing follow-on vehicles, and in 2012 Virgin Galactic bought the remaining 30 percent of the company's shares.

Now to the design. SpaceShipTwo was about twice the size of its predecessor. SpaceShipOne carried one pilot and two passengers, while SpaceShipTwo was designed for two pilots and six passengers. The cabin had large windows, and the seats tilted backward for landing. A carrier aircraft, WhiteKnightTwo, would lift it to about 13,500 meters. After release, it would climb on its hybrid rocket engine. By design, its target altitude was about 110 kilometers, which is 10 kilometers above the Karman line, and its speed was about 4,200 km/h.

The way back was highly unusual. In feathered reentry, the craft folds its wings to slow down, then returns them to normal and glides to a runway landing. In 2008, Burt Rutan said the vehicle was designed to be as safe as the early airliners of the 1920s, and that people should not expect modern airliner safety. Tickets initially cost $200,000. Test flights were from Mojave, while commercial flights were planned to begin from Spaceport America in New Mexico.

Sources differ on one point. One says Virgin ordered five craft, while another says only three had been ordered by 2015. The dream was big, part of the technology came from SpaceShipOne, and the promises were big too. But an accident was soon to change everything.

articleEn: On 26 July 2007, early testing of SpaceShipTwo's systems was under way at Mojave Air and Space Port. The aim was to test components of the rocket motor. A hybrid rocket motor uses a solid fuel and a liquid oxidizer. For SpaceShipTwo the oxidizer was nitrous oxide, and in the early design the fuel was HTPB.

This was an oxidizer flow test. The team filled the oxidizer tank with about 4,500 kg of nitrous oxide, and a 15-second cold-flow injector test was run. A cold-flow test means the nitrous oxide passes through the injectors but is not burned. The method was thought to be safe. But during it, an explosion occurred. The gas had not ignited, yet three Scaled Composites employees were killed and three were injured.

The dead were Todd Ivens, Eric Blackwell and Charles May, and we remember them with full respect. They had been watching the test from behind a chain-link fence, but that fence offered no protection from shrapnel and debris. The company was later fined for violating health and safety rules, and the incident delayed the program. According to reports, the cause of the accident was never made public, so many questions remain open today.

SpaceShipTwo's goal was to take space tourists to the edge of space. In such a project every experiment is delicate, and the 2007 accident was a reminder of that. Developing the rocket motor was already difficult. That same engine would later cause a major delay in the program, which we will look at further on.

Earlier, on 28 September 2006, Richard Branson had presented a mock-up of the SpaceShipTwo passenger cabin at the NextFest exposition in New York, held at the Jacob K. Javits Convention Center. The idea of space tourism was no longer just talk. Then in January 2008, the vehicle's design was shown to the media, and it was said to be about 60 percent complete. In 2008 it was announced that test launches would be from Mojave Spaceport, where Scaled Composites was building the craft, with Spaceport America in New Mexico later becoming the permanent base. Three lives had been lost, but the program moved on. The next big moment would come on 7 December 2009, when SpaceShipTwo was shown to the public.

articleEn: On 7 December 2009, there was a stir at Mojave Air and Space Port. For the first time, SpaceShipTwo was formally rolled out before the world. At the ceremony, California's then governor Arnold Schwarzenegger named the first SpaceShipTwo. It was called VSS Enterprise, a tribute to the fictional starship Enterprise from the Star Trek TV series. The same name had also been given to NASA's prototype Space Shuttle orbiter. 300 guests were present, and each of them had booked a $200,000 ticket for a seat.

On this occasion Richard Branson said that flights would begin in 2011. It was a very big promise, but the older timeline tells a different story. The early plan in 2008 had test flights starting in late 2009 and commercial service in 2011. In reality, captive carry and glide tests began in 2010, and the first rocket-powered flight took place in 2013. The schedule had slipped considerably.

In April 2011, Branson announced further delays. He hoped that about 18 months later he would be heading into space in his spaceship. This was not the first time: in July 2008, too, Branson had said the first space trip would happen within about 18 months. In May 2013, Branson said he would be aboard the first public flight, and a new date of 25 December 2013 was given.

Demand, meanwhile, was not shrinking. Initially, more than 65,000 people applied for the first 100 tickets. By December 2007, 200 customers had paid. By early 2011 the number was 410, and by early 2013 it was 575. In April 2013, Virgin Galactic announced that the price of a seat would rise by 25 percent to $250,000. The ticket-selling network was wide, too, with more than 140 space agents around the world selling tickets. By August 2013, 640 customers had signed up.

But a big question remained: could the craft really be ready on time? Costs were also rising. In 2007, SpaceShipTwo's development cost was estimated at $108 million, but by May 2011 the estimate had reached $400 million. At the end of 2009, the company declined to give a firm date for commercial flights, saying that operational roll-out would follow a safety-driven schedule.
So, whatever the shine of the rollout, the real test was still ahead. The craft had to be flown in the air, and step by step.

articleEn: Now we turn to testing. In October 2009, Virgin Galactic CEO Will Whitehorn described a flight test program of seven stages. First came ground testing, then captive carry under White Knight Two, then unpowered glides, and then subsonic tests with brief rocket firings. After that came supersonic tests, then full flights to suborbital space, and finally a long review with the FAA so that a commercial launch license could be obtained.

On 22 March 2010, VSS Enterprise made its first captive carry flight, in which the mothership VMS Eve carried the craft on a short flight. The second flight, on 16 May 2010, lasted about five hours and went up to launch altitude, 51,000 feet. Its purpose was a cold soak test of the avionics and pressurization system. On 15 July 2010, Enterprise made its first crewed flight. The craft stayed attached to Eve, and the flight lasted 6 hours 21 minutes.

Then came 10 October 2010. Enterprise was released from Eve at 45,000 feet and glided safely to a landing at Mojave. On 4 May 2011, the feathered reentry configuration was tried in the air, a method in which the craft folds its wings on the way back. On 9 June 2011, because of a technical problem, SpaceShipTwo could not separate from White Knight Two. In June there were five successful glide flights, and testing continued.

On the 16th glide flight, on 29 September 2011, the crew briefly lost control of the craft. What happened next? The craft adopted the feathered wing configuration, control was restored, and the crew landed safely after a 7-minute flight. Here, feathering helped.

In June 2012, the FAA granted a permit for rocket-powered supersonic test flights. By September 2012, the unpowered glide program was nearly complete. In December 2012, after the engine was installed, the craft made its first glide flight.

Then came the day everyone had been waiting for. On 29 April 2013, SpaceShipTwo made its first powered test flight. The engine burned for 16 seconds, and the craft climbed from 47,000 feet to 55,000 feet. Branson said the flight could not have been smoother. But not everyone was so reassured. The craft reached Mach 1.2, about 920 mph, which was less than half of the 2,000 mph speed Branson had cited.

On the second powered flight, on 5 September 2013, the craft reached Mach 1.43, climbed to 69,000 feet and returned using feathering. The third powered flight, on 10 January 2014, went higher than before. It tested a new thermal coating on the tail booms and other systems. Yet even by September 2014, the craft had reached only about 71,000 feet, or 13 miles. The FAA license required an altitude of 62 miles.
So the question was, after so many tests, what was the craft still missing? A large part of the answer lay in the story of the engine.

articleEn: Now let's talk about the issue that caused serious delays in the program: SpaceShipTwo's hybrid rocket engine. The original design used a rubber-like fuel called HTPB together with nitrous oxide, and was also called an N2O/HTPB engine. The engine was developed from 2009 to early 2014 by Sierra Nevada Corporation, a subcontractor to Scaled Composites. The problem was that these engines suffered from stability issues on firings of more than about 20 seconds, while the design called for a burn of about 70 seconds.

A big decision came in May 2014. On 23 May, Virgin Galactic announced that Sierra Nevada's nitrous oxide rubber motor had been abandoned. The company took engine development into its own hands and ended Sierra Nevada's contract. Thus all work on the first-generation rocket engine stopped.

The new engine was to use a plastic fuel called thermoplastic polyamide in place of rubber. It was said that this would let the craft reach a higher altitude. By May 2014, the new engine had completed full-duration burns of more than 60 seconds in ground tests. But the craft also had to be modified. Two additional tanks were added to the wings, one with methane and the other with helium, so the new engine could burn and shut down properly.

In September 2014, Branson gave February or March 2015 for the first commercial flight, even though the new plastic fuel had not been burned in any flight. According to Tom Bower, who wrote a book about Branson, a single engine had taken ten years, and going to space in six months with a new engine was not possible. In September 2014, the Sunday Times wrote that Branson was facing a backlash from people who had booked. This reaction came after the announcement of further delays.

The company had collected $80 million in fares and deposits, and people's expectations were tied up with that sum. In October 2014, speaking to the Guardian, CEO George Whitesides said that when he arrived in 2010 the company was mostly a marketing organisation. By his account, the company could now design, build, test and fly its own rocket motor at Mojave.

So the credibility of the old promises had been called into question. The company's position was that its decisions were driven by safety and by completing the flight test program. Then came the date of 31 October 2014.

articleEn: On the morning of 31 October 2014, everything over Mojave seemed routine. This was the fourth powered test flight of VSS Enterprise. The time was 10:51 PST. On this flight, a new plastic-based fuel was being tried for the first time, replacing the old rubber-based solid fuel. According to some sources, the fuel was based on nylon plastic grains. One source says the old fuel had not lived up to expectations.

Enterprise was released from the WhiteKnightTwo mothership, and shortly afterward the engine ignited. According to one report, the craft was at about 50,000 feet at the time. There were two pilots in the cockpit. Peter Siebold, age 43, was pilot in command, and beside him sat 39-year-old co-pilot Michael Alsbury. According to the flight plan, after the rocket fired the craft was to reach supersonic speed, and the time to unlock the feather would come when speed reached Mach 1.4.

But that is not what happened. According to the NTSB, the tail section began to rotate when the craft was at only Mach 1. The later investigation revealed that the co-pilot had unlocked the movable tail section about ten seconds after the rocket fired. At that moment the craft was breaking the speed of sound. Even after unlocking, rotating the tail required a separate pilot command, and that was not given. Yet the tail section rotated anyway.

The feather deployed while the craft was still in powered ascent, meaning the rocket engine was still running. Telemetry and cockpit video showed that the air braking system deployed incorrectly and too early. About two seconds later, the craft began to break apart in the air. According to one report, the anomaly was reported about 60 to 90 seconds after the flight began. The wreckage fell in the Mojave desert. Early reports called it only an in-flight anomaly, and the real cause had to await the investigation.

Peter Siebold managed to get out of the aircraft and reached the ground by parachute. He was the only pilot to survive the accident. Co-pilot Michael Alsbury lost his life in it. He was 39 years old and was also a Scaled Composites employee. According to sources, this was the first spacecraft accident in which part of the crew survived and part did not. Siebold was also described as the only person to survive a spacecraft disintegration.
So what was the moment that changed everything? Was it only a pilot's mistake, or was a bigger problem hidden elsewhere?

chapters.covers: NTSB chairman Christopher Hart on 2 November 2014: engine and tanks intact, no explosion; tail unlocked early and pivoted without a separate command. 28 July 2015 hearing: co-pilot's premature unlock, lack of fail-safe design, poor pilot training, weak FAA oversight, anxious co-pilot without recent flight experience, human factors ignored. Recommendations to the FAA.

articleEn: Friends, after the accident the US National Transportation Safety Board, the NTSB, began an independent investigation. One question was on everyone's mind: why did the craft break apart? The first suspicion could have fallen on the fuel or engine, since this was the first flight of the new plastic fuel. But the initial examination showed something else. The early investigation found that the engine and propellant tanks were intact, so there had been no fuel explosion. Telemetry data and cockpit video showed that the air braking system, the feather, deployed wrongly and too early, and a few seconds later the craft broke up.

On 2 November 2014, Christopher Hart said that the tail system was supposed to be unlocked at about Mach 1.4. But the tail had begun to rotate at Mach 1. Hart also said it was not clear how the tail rotated after unlocking, since that required a separate pilot command, which had not been given. He also raised a question: had the craft's position and speed let the tail swing on its own? At that time it was only an open question.

Then on 28 July 2015, the NTSB held a hearing in Washington D.C. A press release was issued the same day, and the investigation's findings came out. According to the board, the co-pilot unlocked the tail section too early, about ten seconds after the rocket fired, when the craft was breaking the speed of sound.

During this, the NTSB also said something else: the craft's designers had not prepared for the possibility of human error. That is, there was no fail-safe system that could prevent the feather from unlocking too early, or at least discourage it. According to Hart, human factors were not emphasized in the design, safety assessment and operation. In his words, this aspect is important for the safety of human spaceflight.

The NTSB listed several factors: inadequate design safeguards, weak pilot training, and a lack of strong FAA oversight. All of these were considered important factors in the accident. The report also said the co-pilot was possibly anxious and lacked recent flight experience. This was one factor, not the whole story. According to one source, the FAA, its Office of Commercial Space Transportation and the designers were all criticized for not building a fail-safe system.

Scaled Composites' role in the whole story was also important. This Northrop Grumman unit was both the craft's designer and its operator. Now the question was what should be done next. The NTSB recommended that the FAA create special human factors guidance for commercial spaceflight operators. The other recommendation was that the application process for experimental spaceflight permits be made more rigorous, meaning the approval process should be stricter than before.

So what was the outcome? The co-pilot unlocked the feather too early, and the design had no protective net to stop that mistake. But what did Virgin Galactic change after this report? And did everything really change? That is what we will see in the next part.

articleEn: In its submission to the NTSB, Virgin Galactic said that the nearly complete second SpaceShipTwo had been modified with an automatic mechanical inhibit device. This device prevents the feather from being locked or unlocked during safety-critical phases. So a technical answer to this very problem was prepared. A clear warning about the danger of premature unlocking was added to the checklist and operating handbook. A crew resource management approach was also being adopted for SS2. But one thing remained. Virgin confirmed that it would make no change to the cockpit display system, even though CRM issues had been named as a possible cause.

On 19 February 2016, the second SpaceShipTwo, VSS Unity, was unveiled. Ground testing began, and then the first glide flight took place in December 2016. On 13 December 2018, Unity reached an altitude of 82.7 km. By the American definition this was space, but it was below the common 100 km definition. On a flight in February 2019, Unity reached 89.9 km, with three people aboard, including one passenger.

On 11 July 2021, Richard Branson became, by the American definition, the first company founder to go to space aboard his own craft. But on that same flight the craft had left its designated airspace, which the FAA investigated, and flights were paused for a time. On 29 June 2023, the first commercial flight took place with Galactic 01, carrying three outside passengers. It was a 70-minute mission. Then on 8 June 2024, Unity made its last flight with Galactic 07. The company shifted its attention to its next generation, the Delta-class spaceships. According to sources, commercial service from the Delta class was hoped for by 2026, with the stated aim of more flights and better operational efficiency.

So what lesson does this story hold? The first is that human error is always possible, so a design should make mistakes difficult. The second is that safety matters more than schedule promises. The company itself kept saying its decisions were driven by safety, and that should be the standard.

Some questions remained open. At the start, Hart said how the tail rotated was not clear, and Virgin confirmed it would not change the cockpit display system. The memory of Michael Alsbury and the survival of Peter Siebold are the human side of this story. If you liked the video, please like it and subscribe to the channel.

shorts.text: صرف دو seconds میں ایک spaceplane ہوا میں بکھر گیا۔ یہ کیسے ہوا؟ 31 October 2014 کو صبح 10:51 PST پر VSS Enterprise کی چوتھی powered test flight جاری تھی۔ اس flight میں پہلی بار ایک نیا plastic based fuel آزمایا جا رہا تھا۔ Enterprise کو WhiteKnightTwo mothership سے چھوڑا گیا، اور engine ignite ہو گیا۔ Cockpit میں دو pilots تھے۔ 43 سال کے Peter Siebold پائلٹ ان کمانڈ تھے، اور 39 سال کے Michael Alsbury co-pilot۔ پھر descent کے لیے بنا feathering system وقت سے پہلے deploy ہو گیا، جبکہ ship ابھی powered ascent میں تھی۔ تقریباً دو seconds بعد جہاز ٹوٹ گیا۔ Siebold parachute سے اتر آئے، مگر Michael Alsbury اس حادثے میں جان سے گئے۔ آخر feather اتنی جلدی کیسے کھلا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Sirf do seconds mein ek spaceplane hawa mein bikhar gaya. Yeh kaise hua? 31 October 2014 ko subah 10:51 PST par VSS Enterprise ki chauthi powered test flight jari thi. Is flight mein pehli bar ek naya plastic based fuel azmaya ja raha tha. Enterprise ko WhiteKnightTwo mothership se chhora gaya, aur engine ignite ho gaya. Cockpit mein do pilots thay. 43 saal ke Peter Siebold pilot in command thay, aur 39 saal ke Michael Alsbury co-pilot. Phir descent ke liye bana feathering system waqt se pehle deploy ho gaya, jabke ship abhi powered ascent mein thi. Taqriban do seconds baad jahaz toot gaya. Siebold parachute se utar aaye, magar Michael Alsbury is hadse mein jaan se gaye. Aakhir feather itni jaldi kaise khula? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.

shorts.titleEn: The 'Safe' Test That Cost Three Lives in 2007
shorts.text: ایک test جسے محفوظ سمجھا جا رہا تھا، تین جانیں لے گیا۔ یہ کہانی ہے 26 July 2007 کی۔ Mojave Air and Space Port پر SpaceShipTwo کے rocket motor کے پرزوں کی testing ہو رہی تھی۔ یہ oxidizer flow test تھا۔ Team نے tank میں تقریباً 4,500 kg nitrous oxide بھری، اور پھر 15 seconds کا cold-flow injector test کیا گیا۔ Cold-flow کا مطلب ہے کہ gas injectors سے گزرتی ہے، مگر اسے جلایا نہیں جاتا۔ اس طریقے کو محفوظ سمجھا جا رہا تھا۔ لیکن اسی دوران explosion ہو گیا۔ Gas ignite نہیں ہوئی تھی، پھر بھی Scaled Composites کے تین employees، Todd Ivens، Eric Blackwell اور Charles May، جان سے گئے، اور تین دوسرے زخمی ہوئے۔ ایک source کے مطابق اس کی وجہ آج تک عام نہیں کی گئی۔ تو سوال یہ ہے کہ program پھر آگے کیسے بڑھا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek test jise mehfooz samjha ja raha tha, teen jaanein le gaya. Yeh kahani hai 26 July 2007 ki. Mojave Air and Space Port par SpaceShipTwo ke rocket motor ke purzon ki testing ho rahi thi. Yeh oxidizer flow test tha. Team ne tank mein taqriban 4,500 kg nitrous oxide bhari, aur phir 15 seconds ka cold-flow injector test kiya gaya. Cold-flow ka matlab hai ke gas injectors se guzarti hai, magar ise jalaya nahin jata. Is tareeqe ko mehfooz samjha ja raha tha. Lekin isi doran explosion ho gaya. Gas ignite nahin hui thi, phir bhi Scaled Composites ke teen employees, Todd Ivens, Eric Blackwell aur Charles May, jaan se gaye, aur teen doosre zakhmi hue. Ek source ke mutabiq is ki wajah aaj tak aam nahin ki gayi. To sawal yeh hai ke program phir aage kaise barha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn: On 26 July 2007, a cold-flow test of SpaceShipTwo's rocket motor components ended in an explosion at Mojave. Three Scaled Composites employees lost their lives.

shorts.titleEn: Did the Fuel Explode? What NTSB Really Found
shorts.text: سب کو لگا کہ نیا fuel پھٹ گیا ہوگا۔ مگر کیا واقعی ایسا تھا؟ Hادثے کے بعد NTSB نے آزاد تحقیق شروع کی۔ ابتدائی جانچ میں پتا چلا کہ engine اور propellant tanks سلامت تھے، یعنی کوئی fuel explosion نہیں ہوا تھا۔ Telemetry data اور cockpit video نے دکھایا کہ feather وقت سے پہلے کھل گیا۔ 2 November 2014 کو Christopher Hart نے بتایا کہ tail کو تقریباً Mach 1.4 پر unlock ہونا تھا، مگر وہ Mach 1 پر ہی گھومنے لگی۔ پھر 28 July 2015 کو NTSB نے کہا کہ co-pilot نے rocket fire ہونے کے تقریباً دس seconds بعد tail section کو وقت سے پہلے unlock کر دیا۔ Board نے design کو بھی ذمہ دار ٹھہرایا، کیونکہ اس میں انسانی غلطی سے بچانے والا fail-safe system نہیں تھا۔ تو اس کے بعد Virgin Galactic نے کیا بدلا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Sab ko laga ke naya fuel phat gaya hoga. Magar kya waqai aisa tha? Hadse ke baad NTSB ne azad tehqeeq shuru ki. Ibtidai jaanch mein pata chala ke engine aur propellant tanks salamat thay, yaani koi fuel explosion nahin hua tha. Telemetry data aur cockpit video ne dikhaya ke feather waqt se pehle khul gaya. 2 November 2014 ko Christopher Hart ne bataya ke tail ko taqriban Mach 1.4 par unlock hona tha, magar woh Mach 1 par hi ghoomne lagi. Phir 28 July 2015 ko NTSB ne kaha ke co-pilot ne rocket fire hone ke taqriban das seconds baad tail section ko waqt se pehle unlock kar diya. Board ne design ko bhi zimmedar thehraya, kyunke is mein insani ghalti se bachane wala fail-safe system nahin tha. To is ke baad Virgin Galactic ne kya badla? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn: The NTSB found no fuel explosion in the VSS Enterprise breakup. Its 2015 report pointed to premature feather unlocking and a design without fail-safes.
